proposals.relationship: White credits Giddens with helping him understand cultural persistence and change as products of active transmission rather than opposites.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2021 written answer, read in Fontella’s Portuguese translation published 2022:13 and 16, explicitly gives Giddens greater weight than Wagner and describes the lens used to study Indigenous–European cultural change. At 16 he connects structuration with his criticism of upstreaming. The interviewer supplies the 1979/1981/1984 work dates; this answer does not independently identify which individual book supplied each insight. No fresh reading of Giddens’s originals, formal teaching or complete adherence is inferred.

proposals.relationship: White acknowledges Lévi-Strauss’s earlier influence and adapts bricolage and cross-cultural coalition while qualifying his structuralist typologies.
proposals.evidence_note: Own complete 2011 preface: xiii/note 2, xvii–xix/notes 18–27 and xxiv expressly recalls substantial influence, admires his conceptual boldness, and develops particular resources from The Savage Mind and Race and History. White distinguishes these uses from rejection of rigid historical/ahistorical divisions; influence and criticism coexist. The editions cited in the preface and the 1952 pamphlet remain White’s references, not newly read originals; the 2011 retrospective is distinct from the 1991 book.

proposals.relationship: White rejects rigid hot/cold social typologies and extends bricolage beyond a closed inventory of inherited cultural materials.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2011:xvii–xix distinguishes the more schematic structuralist readings from Lévi-Strauss’s own changing, nuanced statements. White’s hybrid societies can consciously create new rituals and structures; bricolage can incorporate new scientific elements. This is a specific disagreement with categorical and closed-system versions, alongside acknowledged debt and shared cross-cultural concerns, not a claim that Lévi-Strauss denied all historical change. Own translated 2021 answer at 2022:14 restates that qualification; underlying works remain unread.

proposals.relationship: White uses Scott’s account of households, unstable alliances and refuges from state power to sharpen the comparative possibilities of the middle ground.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2011:xiv explicitly recalls admiring and using Scott, then credits The Art of Not Being Governed with developing a more theoretically powerful comparative account than his own earlier empiricism. Notes 6–9 identify Scott 2009:38, ix, 129–137 and 210–211. The specific interpretation is White’s substantive reading, not a fresh reading of Scott’s full book or evidence that the 2009 work caused White’s 1991 argument.

proposals.relationship: In White’s account, Scott develops his earlier attention to households and provisional village alliances into a wider comparative analysis of state-resistant refuges.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2011:xiv reports Scott’s explicit credit at The Art of Not Being Governed 2009:38, then explains how Scott uses that insight differently and more effectively across Zomia and other regions. This is a relationship mediated through White’s named substantive discussion of Scott; the original Scott passage and full book are unread. It does not equate the pays d’en haut with Zomia or infer identical arguments or personal contact.

proposals.relationship: Deloria questions whether the middle ground’s metaphor and dependence on balanced power limit its portability as an analytic concept.
proposals.evidence_note: Own complete 2006:15–22 distinguishes his admiration for White’s detailed research and cultural-production argument from concern about simplification, place/process slippage and a structural-equivalence requirement. At 21–22 he seeks more complex theories of power, and allows that new cultural production travels beyond the pays d’en haut; this is not a rejection of all comparison. White 2011:xii/note 1 explicitly credits Deloria’s sympathetic criticism with clarification. Existing White-to-Deloria writing-resource edge_2617 remains unchanged, with no second contribution arrow in that direction.

proposals.relationship: White challenges Hofstadter’s account of Gilded Age individualism and weak government, emphasizing household ideals, cooperation and state intervention.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Stanford interview, question on earlier historical interpretations and the following question on misconceptions, names Hofstadter jointly with Wiebe on laissez-faire, corruption and weak government, then singles out Hofstadter on individualism. White instead describes tariffs, subsidies and social provision, power delegated without sufficient administrative capacity, and the home as a political ideal. These are White’s attributed objections, not proof that every Hofstadter text neglects government or cooperation. Existing Wiebe critique edge_2340 retains its joint-target qualifications; complete monographs remain unread. Department repost dated 25 October 2017 is distinct from the linked original News Service item.
